I cannot help launch a real hoax or target a real community. For a fictional tabletop, though, an incident brief can show the shape of the abuse while keeping names, domains, copy, and distribution channels inert. In the exercise, call the site Northbridge Bulletin and make the affected service a fictional municipal ferry. The artifact should be hosted only in a closed training environment and every page should carry an unmistakable exercise watermark.

The first phase of the scenario is preparation. The fictional operator chooses a name that sounds like a local news outlet, borrows generic visual conventions such as a masthead, a timestamp, and a prominent update banner, and builds a landing page with a headline, a short explanation, and a link to an alleged official notice. For training purposes, the link should resolve to a harmless evidence page rather than collect credentials or redirect visitors. The exercise packet can give analysts the page title, certificate issuance time, registrar data, and a screenshot, so they practice comparing those clues with the legitimate agency website.

The second phase is distribution. A small set of fictional accounts posts the same claim at staggered times, while a facilitator injects screenshots into a simulated group chat and local forum. The narrative becomes more believable when the messages repeat a concrete but unverifiable detail, cite an unnamed staff member, and use a countdown to encourage forwarding. Those features should be represented only as redacted examples; do not provide copy that could be reused against a real audience. The scenario can still ask trainees to identify the emotional trigger, the missing source, and the point at which repetition is being mistaken for confirmation.

The third phase introduces corrections and pressure. The official agency publishes a conflicting statement, some participants demand certainty, and a journalist asks for comment. Trainees must preserve the page and message timestamps, contact the real agency through a known number, publish a correction without repeating the false headline unnecessarily, and report the domain and accounts through established channels. They should also consider accessibility, translation, and people who do not use social media.

This format teaches the recognizable mechanics of credibility laundering, coordinated repetition, and urgency without turning the exercise into a deployable campaign. The useful outcome is a tested verification and response process, not a more persuasive hoax.
